title: Hot partitions, rebalancing and resharding without downtime
scopeHtml:
Scope: hot keys, rebalancing strategies, online resharding, capacity planning.

Scope: hot keys, rebalancing strategies, online resharding, capacity planning.

notes.title: What a hot partition is
notes.html:
A hot partition is one shard that receives far more traffic than the others, so it becomes the bottleneck while the rest sit idle. Adding more shards does not help because the extra capacity is not where the load is.

Causes:

  • Hot key: one celebrity user, one viral product, one flash-sale item.
  • Skewed key distribution: sequential keys on range partitions, one giant tenant.
  • Time-based hotspot: everyone reads "today's" partition.
  • Bad hashing luck: a few shards randomly get more big keys.

How it looks in production: one node at 95% CPU while the cluster averages 20%; p99 latency spikes on a subset of requests; throttling errors on one partition (DynamoDB ProvisionedThroughputExceededException even though table-level capacity looks fine); one Redis node with a huge instantaneous_ops_per_sec.

Worked example. A cluster of 10 shards each handling up to 10k ops/s (100k total). A viral post gets 40k reads/s, all on its single shard: that shard saturates at 10k and drops 75% of requests, while the cluster as a whole uses only 40% of its capacity.

Industry examples. Twitter faced celebrity accounts (very high fan-out); Instagram handles celebrity feeds differently from normal users; DynamoDB documents "hot partitions" and added adaptive capacity to shift throughput to hot partitions (confirm limits in current docs, one partition is still capped at about 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second).

Everyday analogy. A supermarket with 10 checkout lanes where everyone queues at lane 3 because the only cashier who sells lottery tickets sits there.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling it a capacity problem and answering "add shards".
  • Not distinguishing a hot key (cannot be split by hashing) from a hot range (can be split).
  • Not naming the metric: per-partition ops, not cluster average.

notes.title: Detecting and fixing hot keys
notes.html:
Detection: per-key counters sampled (Redis redis-cli --hotkeys needs an LFU policy; MONITOR is too expensive in prod), per-partition metrics, proxy-level sampling (Twemproxy, Envoy), top-N sketches (count-min sketch) in the app.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  1. Cache in front. A local in-process cache with a 1 to 5 s TTL on the hot key removes most reads.
  2. Replicate the hot key. Store copies under key#0 .. key#9; readers pick a random one. Reads spread over 10 shards.
  3. Salting writes. For a counter, write to likes:post42:{0..9} randomly and sum on read (or aggregate in the background). Writes spread; reads cost 10 lookups or a periodic rollup.
  4. Request coalescing (single-flight). On cache miss only one request goes to the database; others wait for it. Prevents stampedes.
  5. Isolate: put the known whale on its own shard (directory-based mapping).
  6. Queue and batch writes. Buffer increments and flush every second.
import random
N = 10  # copies of the hot key
def read_hot(key):
    return redis.get(f"{key}#{random.randrange(N)}")
def write_hot(key, val):
    for i in range(N):
        redis.set(f"{key}#{i}", val)

Worked example. A flash-sale product row gets 30k reads/s on one MySQL shard. Add a 2 s local cache across 50 app servers: each server hits the DB at most 0.5 times/s for that key, so about 25 reads/s total (a 1,200x reduction). Stale for at most 2 s, acceptable for a product page, not for stock count at checkout.

Decision gravity. Key replication and salting are reversible app-level changes, but add read or write amplification and consistency complexity. Cache is the cheapest. Isolating a tenant via directory is also reversible.

Industry examples. Memcached/Facebook "leases" prevent thundering herd; Redis Cluster users often append hash tags or random suffixes; Discord coalesces identical requests to Cassandra in its data services so a hot channel produces one query.

Everyday analogy. Printing 10 copies of the popular notice and pinning them in different corridors instead of one on the main door.

Common interview traps.

  • Salting counters and forgetting the read cost.
  • Caching hot items without TTL or invalidation thinking, then serving stale prices.
  • Not mentioning the cache stampede when a hot key expires.

notes.title: Rebalancing: moving data between shards
notes.html:
Rebalancing moves partitions from busy or full nodes to others, after nodes are added, removed or the load shifts. The constraints: keep serving traffic, limit network use, and not lose or duplicate writes.

Strategies:

  • Fixed number of partitions (many more partitions than nodes): create, say, 1,024 partitions up front; a new node steals some partitions whole. Used by Elasticsearch (primary shard count fixed at index creation), Kafka (partitions), Riak, Couchbase (vBuckets), Redis Cluster (slots).
  • Dynamic splitting: a partition splits when it grows past a size (for example 10 GB) or load. HBase, Bigtable, MongoDB chunks (balancer migrates chunks), CockroachDB ranges (512 MiB default range size, confirm in docs).
  • Proportional to nodes: Cassandra vnodes: each new node takes random token ranges.

Automatic vs manual: automatic rebalancing is convenient but can surprise you, because moving data during a load spike makes the spike worse and a falsely detected node failure can trigger a storm of copying. Many teams require a human to approve or throttle.

Worked example. 3 nodes with 48 partitions total (16 each), 300 GB each. Add node D: target is 12 each, so each old node gives 4 partitions (about 75 GB), 225 GB moves in total. On a 1 Gbps (about 100 MB/s usable) link capped at 50% for the migration: 225,000 MB / 50 MB/s = 4,500 s, about 75 minutes. Throttle with stream_throughput_outbound (Cassandra) or MongoDB balancer windows.

# MongoDB: only balance at night
mongosh --eval 'db.getSiblingDB("config").settings.updateOne(
  {_id:"balancer"},
  {$set:{activeWindow:{start:"01:00",stop:"05:00"}}}, {upsert:true})'

Decision gravity. Over-provisioning partitions up front (fixed count) is cheap insurance and reversible. Too many partitions add overhead (each Kafka partition and Elasticsearch shard costs memory and file handles); too few caps parallelism forever. Elasticsearch fixed primary shard count is effectively a one-way door (needs reindex or split API).

Industry examples. Kafka partition reassignment (kafka-reassign-partitions.sh, Cruise Control automates it), Elasticsearch shard allocation, MongoDB balancer, Cassandra nodetool rebuild/bootstrap, CockroachDB automatic range rebalancing.

Everyday analogy. Moving students from crowded classrooms to a new classroom by whole benches, not by tearing benches apart.

Common interview traps.

  • Using hash % N and then proposing to "just add a node".
  • Ignoring that rebalancing competes with live traffic for disk and network.
  • Setting 10,000 tiny partitions "to be safe", producing overhead.

notes.title: Resharding without downtime
notes.html:
Resharding means changing how data is split (more shards, or a different key) while the system stays up. The standard pattern is dual write plus backfill plus cutover:

  1. Provision new shards (target layout).
  2. Backfill: copy existing data from old shards to new in the background, throttled. Take a consistent snapshot or record the position (binlog/WAL offset).
  3. Catch up: stream changes since the snapshot (CDC with Debezium, Vitess VReplication, MongoDB change streams) so new shards track old ones.
  4. Verify: compare row counts and checksums; optionally shadow-read from the new shards and diff results.
  5. Cutover: briefly stop writes (seconds) or use a routing flag per shard, flip reads then writes to the new layout.
  6. Keep old as fallback (reverse replication) for days, then delete.

Variations:

  • Split in place (doubling): each old shard splits into two, children get half the hash range. Easy with power-of-two logical shards because every key's new home is deterministic. Instagram-style logical shards are designed so physical moves only copy a logical shard.
  • Double-write at app level: the app writes to both old and new for the new key space. Simple but you must handle partial failures (write to old succeeds, new fails) via outbox/retry.
  • Feature flag per tenant/key range to migrate gradually and roll back one at a time.

Worked example. Move from 4 to 8 shards, 2 TB total. Backfill 500 GB per old shard at 40 MB/s = about 3.5 hours each; CDC lag shrinks to under 1 s; cutover with a 3-second write pause per shard behind a router flag (flip shard_map.state from MIGRATING to ACTIVE). Total user-visible disruption: a few seconds of elevated latency per shard.

# Vitess-style MoveTables workflow (illustrative stages)
steps:
  - create: copy schema to target keyspace
  - vreplication: copy plus stream binlog
  - verify: VDiff compare
  - switch_reads
  - switch_writes
  - complete: drop source

Industry examples. Vitess MoveTables/Reshard, Stripe's online migration approach (dual writes, shadow reads, then cutover), Shopify's pod mobility moves shops between database pods with minimal downtime using Ghostferry, Notion's 2021 resharding from 32 to 480 logical shards using Postgres logical replication, GitHub gh-ost for online schema change.

Decision gravity. Dual write and CDC are reversible until the cutover step; cutover is the commit point, so keep reverse replication ready. Changing the shard key (rather than the count) is the hardest, because all queries and indexes change; it is a one-way door in practice.

Everyday analogy. Moving house while living there: carry boxes over a few weeks, keep both addresses working, then switch the mail forwarding on one day.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting writes that happen during backfill (need CDC or dual write).
  • No verification step before cutover.
  • No rollback plan.
  • Dual writes without handling partial failure (use outbox or CDC instead).

notes.title: Capacity planning to avoid emergencies
notes.html:
Reshard before you must. Resharding under load, with a full disk, is how outages happen.

Rules of thumb:

  • Alert at 60% of disk, CPU or write IOPS per shard, act at 70%. Resharding takes days to weeks to plan; the data copy needs headroom itself.
  • Pick the logical shard count generously (1,024 or 4,096) so you scale from 4 to 64 machines without changing mapping.
  • Watch growth: with 15% month-on-month data growth, 60% full turns into 100% full in about 4 months.
  • Test the runbook: rehearse resharding on a copy in staging at production scale.
  • Keep a per-shard dashboard: size, QPS, p99, replication lag, top keys.

Worked example. Shard at 1.8 TB of 3 TB disk, growing 100 GB/week: 12 weeks to full. Backfill takes 2 weeks and planning 2 weeks, so start now, not when the alert pages at 90%.

Industry examples. Notion reportedly resharded when Postgres hit vacuum and disk limits; Figma and Slack describe vertical sharding and logical shards as ways to buy time; Pinterest's early sharding used pre-created virtual shards (made when launched) mapped to few servers.

Everyday analogy. Booking a bigger flat before the baby arrives, not the week after.

Common interview traps.

  • Waiting for the disk to fill.
  • Treating resharding as one script instead of a multi-week project with verification and rollback.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Hot partitions come from hot keys, skewed ranges, or time hotspots; more shards do not fix a single hot key.
  • Fix order: cache, replicate hot keys, salt writes, coalesce requests, isolate whales, batch writes.
  • Rebalance with many fixed partitions or dynamic splitting; throttle it and compute the data volume and time.
  • Reshard online: snapshot plus backfill, CDC catch-up, verify, cutover, keep reverse path, then delete.
  • Plan capacity early: alert at 60%, over-provision logical shards, rehearse the runbook.

questions.promptHtml: What is a hot partition, what causes it, and why does adding shards not fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about per-partition load instead of cluster averages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A hot partition is one shard getting far more traffic than the rest, so it saturates while the others idle. Causes are a hot key (a celebrity or viral item), skewed distribution (sequential keys on a range partition, one giant tenant), time hotspots (everyone reads today) and plain bad hashing luck. More shards do not help because the extra capacity is not where the load is; one key always lives on one shard.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: 10 shards, each good for 10k ops/s (100k total). A viral post gets 40k reads/s, all on one shard. That shard drops 75% of requests while the cluster uses 40% of its capacity.

Shard 1: 5k ops/s   (50%)
Shard 2: 5k ops/s   (50%)
Shard 3: 40k ops/s  (400% of capacity)  <- hot

Symptoms: one node at 95% CPU while the average is 20%; p99 spikes for a subset of requests; throttling on one partition (DynamoDB ProvisionedThroughputExceededException while table capacity looks fine; one partition is still capped at about 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second, verify in current docs); a single Redis node with huge instantaneous_ops_per_sec.

Distinguish a hot range (can be split) from a hot key (cannot be split by hashing).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Answering "add shards".
  • Looking only at cluster-average metrics.
  • Treating a hot key like a hot range.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which metric catches it? -> Per-partition ops, CPU and latency, plus top-N key sampling.
  2. Does DynamoDB adaptive capacity solve it? -> It shifts throughput toward hot partitions but a single key is still bounded.
  3. Hot range vs hot key? -> Range: split it. Key: cache, replicate or salt.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "uneven load". The senior distinguishes key vs range, names per-partition metrics and the fix order.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flash sale hit one product row; the 32-shard cluster looked 15% busy while checkout failed.

questions.promptHtml: Name your toolbox for a hot key, in the order you would try it, with the cost of each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior has an ordered playbook and knows each fix's side effects.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cheapest first: cache in front with a short TTL, replicate the hot key under several names and read a random copy, salt counter writes across N sub-keys and sum on read, coalesce requests so a miss hits the database once, isolate the whale on its own shard, and queue and batch writes. Each fix trades something: staleness, read amplification, or complexity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Cache: a 2 s local cache across 50 app servers lowers a 30k reads/s hot key to about 25 reads/s at the database (50 servers at 0.5 reads/s). Stale up to 2 s.
  • Replicate: key#0..key#9; read picks one randomly; writes update all 10 (write amplification).
  • Salt writes: likes:post42:{0..9}; writes spread, reads cost 10 lookups or a periodic rollup.
  • Single-flight: one in-flight load per key; the rest wait.
  • Isolate: directory maps the whale to its own shard.
  • Batch: buffer increments and flush each second.
import random
N = 10  # copies of the hot key
def read_hot(key):
    return redis.get(f"{key}#{random.randrange(N)}")
def write_hot(key, val):
    for i in range(N):
        redis.set(f"{key}#{i}", val)

Detection: redis-cli --hotkeys (needs an LFU policy; MONITOR is too expensive in production), proxy sampling, count-min sketch in the app.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Salting counters and forgetting the read cost.
  • Cache with no invalidation thinking (stale prices at checkout).
  • Forgetting the stampede when the hot key expires.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you stop a stampede? -> Single-flight, jittered TTLs, probabilistic early refresh, leases.
  2. Is salting reversible? -> Yes, app-level change, but data must be merged.
  3. When is staleness unacceptable? -> Stock count at checkout, balances; read those from the source.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use a cache". The senior orders the fixes, states staleness/amplification cost and covers detection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A like counter on one Redis key capped at 80k ops/s; salting to 16 sub-keys gave 1M likes/s.

questions.contextHtml:
A DynamoDB table (provisioned at 20,000 RCU, evenly across about 10 partitions) holds user profiles. A celebrity posts and their profile gets 8,000 reads/s. Errors appear immediately:

ProvisionedThroughputExceededException  (for ~85% of requests on userId=celeb_77)
Table consumed RCU: 11,000 / 20,000
CloudWatch: ThrottledRequests spikes, ReadThrottleEvents on one partition

The on-call proposes doubling the provisioned capacity to 40,000 RCU.
questions.promptHtml: Why does doubling not fix it, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Doubles capacity; costs twice as much and the throttling continues.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it one key? Are reads strongly consistent (costs 2x)? Can this profile be cached for a few seconds?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a short-TTL cache (CDN/DAX/in-process) in front of the profile read; use eventually consistent reads (half the RCU).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) hot key on a single partition limited to about 3,000 RCU (verify current limit) (matches: table at 55% but throttling); b) bad provisioning; c) bursty traffic (burst credits drained).
  4. How I'd verify each: CloudWatch Contributor Insights on the table shows the top keys; check per-partition throttles.
  5. Root cause: Capacity is divided per partition and one key cannot spread across partitions; table-level capacity is irrelevant.
  6. Fix: Short term: cache with 2 to 5 s TTL: 8,000 reads/s becomes roughly the number of cache nodes divided by TTL. Long term: replicate the item as celeb_77#0..9 for known whales, or serve celebrity profiles from a CDN.
  7. Prevention: Contributor Insights alarms, load tests with skewed keys, a "whale list" with special handling.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not double capacity (costly, no effect), and I would not use strong reads for a profile page.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if profile edits must show instantly? -> Invalidate the cache on write; accept a brief stale window for others.
  • What if it were writes? -> Salt or queue and batch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled capacity twice before someone looked at partition metrics; the bill grew, the throttling did not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: doubles capacity.
  • Hire: identifies the hot key and adds a cache.
  • Strong hire: uses per-key insights, replicas for whales and consistency trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A like counter for viral posts was salted across 10 sub-keys to spread writes. After launch: post pages sometimes show "0 likes" for a few seconds, the like count goes backwards, and the read path adds 10 round trips (p99 from 4 ms to 38 ms). Code:

void like(String postId) {
    int salt = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10);
    redis.incr("likes:" + postId + ":" + salt);
}
long count(String postId) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        String v = redis.get("likes:" + postId + ":" + i);
        sum += (v == null) ? 0 : Long.parseLong(v);
    }
    return sum;
}
fun like(postId: String) {
    val salt = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10)
    redis.incr("likes:$postId:$salt")
}
fun count(postId: String): Long =
    (0 until 10).sumOf { redis.get("likes:$postId:$it")?.toLong() ?: 0L }

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a Lua script" without addressing read amplification or why counts go backwards.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the count be exact? Do all posts need salting or only viral ones? Are the 10 keys on different Redis nodes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the summed value for 1 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) 10 sequential GETs are not atomic, and a key expiring or a failover on one slot yields partial sums (explains "0" and backwards); b) read amplification (10 round trips); c) all posts salted though only a few are hot.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at Redis latency by command, compare sums before and after a node failover, count which posts exceed 5k writes/s.
  5. Root cause: Salting moves cost from writes to reads and the multi-key read is not a snapshot.
  6. Fix: Use MGET (one round trip; with Redis Cluster use hash tags so keys are co-located, but that re-creates the hot slot, so instead pipeline per node). Better: a background aggregator rolls sub-counters into likes:post:total every second and readers read the total. Salt only posts flagged hot (for example above 2k writes/s), default to 1 key.
  7. Prevention: Tests for failover and eviction (no TTL/eviction on counters), metrics on salt keys per post.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The rollup makes counts about 1 s stale, fine for likes, not for inventory. I would not use hash tags to put all salts on one node.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need exact count for billing? -> Count from an append-only log (Kafka) with periodic aggregation, not Redis.
  • What if Redis restarts? -> Counters need persistence (AOF) or periodic reconciliation from the source of truth.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A counter salted 64 ways became 64 reads per page view; switching to a 1 s rollup halved Redis CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot see the amplification.
  • Hire: MGET or rollup and selective salting.
  • Strong hire: explains non-atomic reads, cluster slot placement and exactness trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A 3-node Cassandra-like cluster, 300 GB per node, 48 partitions (16 per node). Disks 70% full, so you add node D. Link: 1 Gbps (about 100 MB/s usable). Daytime traffic already uses 60% of the network. Your manager asks "how long and when?"
questions.promptHtml: How much data moves, how long will it take, and how do you run it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It will be done in a few minutes" or "just add the node and let it stream at full speed".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the partition count fixed? Are replicas counted in the 300 GB? What is the latency SLO during the move?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what could go wrong): a) streaming saturates the network and disks, raising p99; b) compaction piles up on the new node; c) a node failing mid-stream.
  4. How I'd verify each: Watch nodetool netstats, disk IO, p99 per node, pending compactions.
  5. Root cause (math): Target 12 partitions per node, so each old node gives 4 (about 75 GB), 225 GB moves total. At 50% of 100 MB/s = 50 MB/s: 225,000 / 50 = 4,500 s, about 75 minutes. If only 40 MB/s is free during the day (60% already used), about 94 minutes; at night with 80 MB/s, about 47 minutes.
  6. Fix (plan): Run at night, cap streaming (nodetool setstreamthroughput or stream_throughput_outbound), add one node at a time, pause on p99 breach, verify with nodetool status and repair after. Reduce disk pressure after the move with nodetool cleanup on old nodes.
  7. Prevention: Add nodes at 60% disk, not 70%; the runbook with rehearsed timings.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Throttling makes it slower but safer; I would not bootstrap multiple nodes at once and not start at 90% disk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Disk is 95% full? -> Cleanup first (compaction needs headroom), or add a node immediately but expect a slow move.
  • With hash % N instead of partitions? -> You would move 75% of the data (3 to 4 nodes), about 675 GB.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bootstrap at 85% disk failed halfway because compaction needed temporary space; the node had to be wiped and redone.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers.
  • Hire: computes 225 GB and a realistic duration with throttling.
  • Strong hire: schedules by traffic, mentions cleanup/compaction headroom and compares to modulo.

questions.contextHtml:
A flash-sale product page reads product:991 from Redis (TTL 60 s) and falls back to MySQL. At peak, 30,000 reads/s. Every 60 s the DB connection pool (200) saturates for about 3 seconds; p99 jumps to 4 s and 2% of requests fail. Logs:

12:00:00.000 cache MISS product:991 (expired)
12:00:00.001..12:00:00.040  4,100 concurrent DB queries for product:991
mysql: Threads_running = 198, Aborted_connects rising

Red herring: the DB slow log shows the query itself takes only 6 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the pattern and design a fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL" (delays but does not remove it) or "add DB connections" (more load, same stampede).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the page be stale a few seconds? Do all app servers use the same key and TTL? Is there a local cache?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add random jitter to the TTL and a short stale-while-revalidate window, so the key never expires for everyone at once.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) cache stampede (thundering herd) on a hot key expiry (matches 4,100 concurrent identical queries); b) slow query (ruled out, 6 ms); c) connection leak.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count identical in-flight queries at expiry, DB performance_schema for statement digests, pool metrics.
  5. Root cause: At the instant of expiry every request misses and each goes to the database; 30,000 req/s times 40 ms of miss window is about 1,200 queries, far above what 200 connections handle.
  6. Fix: Single-flight (one loader per key per process, the rest wait on its result), plus a distributed lock or lease for cross-server coordination, plus serve-stale-while-revalidate: return the old value while one worker refreshes. Add a 2 s local in-process cache.
Future<Product> inflight = loads.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> executor.submit(() -> db.load(k)));
Product p = inflight.get();  // all waiters share one DB call
loads.remove(id);
val inflight = loads.computeIfAbsent(id) { executor.submit(Callable { db.load(id) }) }
val p = inflight.get()  // all waiters share one DB call
loads.remove(id)
  1. Prevention: Load tests with expiry events, jittered TTLs by default, dashboard of concurrent identical queries.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Serving stale means up to a few seconds old (not for stock at checkout, which reads authoritative inventory). I would not set TTL to infinity without explicit invalidation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Single-flight is per process; 50 servers still send 50 queries? -> Yes, 50 queries is fine; use a lock or lease for the cluster if needed.
  • What about invalidation on price change? -> Publish an event to refresh, not delete, the key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A product launch crashed at exactly each minute boundary; a jittered TTL and stale-while-revalidate ended the saw-tooth.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases pool or TTL only.
  • Hire: names stampede and uses single-flight plus jitter.
  • Strong hire: stale-while-revalidate, lease, distinguishes checkout reads and verifies via in-flight query counts.

questions.promptHtml: Compare fixed-partition, dynamic-splitting and proportional (vnode) rebalancing. Should rebalancing be automatic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows if you understand how real systems grow and why rebalancing can hurt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fixed partitions: create many more partitions than nodes up front and let a new node steal whole partitions (Kafka, Redis slots, Couchbase vBuckets, Elasticsearch primary shards). Dynamic splitting: a partition splits when it passes a size or load threshold (HBase, Bigtable, MongoDB chunks, CockroachDB ranges). Proportional: each new node takes random token ranges (Cassandra vnodes). Automatic rebalancing is convenient but can worsen a load spike or storm after a false failure, so many teams throttle or require approval.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy Strength Weakness
Fixed count simple, whole-partition moves wrong count is permanent; too many partitions cost memory/file handles, too few cap parallelism
Dynamic split adapts to data size split/merge churn, hot start for an empty table (pre-split)
Proportional smooth, no coordination of sizes random ranges can be uneven 
Node A (16 partitions) -> Node D (steals 4)
Node B (16 partitions) -> Node D (steals 4)
Node C (16 partitions) -> Node D (steals 4)

Rebalancing competes with live traffic for disk and network. Always throttle, limit concurrent moves, and use maintenance windows (MongoDB balancer active window). Elasticsearch's primary shard count is fixed at index creation, so it is effectively a one-way door (needs reindex or the split API).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• hash % N plus "just add a node".
  • Ignoring the cost to live traffic.
  • Thousands of tiny partitions "to be safe".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many partitions to pre-create? -> Enough for the max node count (for example 1,024 for 4 to 64 machines), not 100k.
  2. Why can auto-rebalancing cause an outage? -> A false node-down detection triggers mass copying that loads the survivors.
  3. How do you rebalance without moving data? -> Move hot partitions' replicas or leaders only, or split the hot range.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists names. The senior gives trade-offs, the over-partitioning rule of thumb and throttling practice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An automatic rebalance during a traffic spike pushed p99 from 20 ms to 900 ms until the balancer was paused.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the standard pattern for resharding a live system with no downtime, and where it can go wrong.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common senior design question about sharding: a safe migration.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Provision the new layout, backfill existing data from a consistent snapshot, stream changes since the snapshot with CDC so the new shards stay current, verify with counts and checksums (and optionally shadow reads), then cut over behind a router flag, with a brief write pause. Keep reverse replication to the old layout for days as a rollback, then delete. The usual failures: missing writes during backfill, no verification, no rollback and dual writes with partial failures.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Old shard -> CDC stream ------> New shard
Old shard -> Backfill copy ---> New shard
App router -> Old shard (until cutover)
  1. Provision new shards. 2. Backfill, throttled, record the binlog/WAL position. 3. Catch up with CDC (Debezium, Vitess VReplication, Mongo change streams). 4. Verify (row counts, checksums such as VDiff, shadow-read diffs). 5. Cutover: flip reads, then writes, per shard, with a brief pause. 6. Keep old as fallback.

Variants: split in place by doubling with power-of-two logical shards (each key's new home is deterministic), app-level dual writes (needs outbox/retry for partial failures), per-tenant feature flags to migrate gradually.

# Vitess MoveTables stages (illustrative)
steps:
  - create: copy schema to target
  - vreplication: copy + stream binlog
  - verify: VDiff
  - switch_reads
  - switch_writes
  - complete

Changing the shard key (not just the count) is the hardest case and effectively a one-way door.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting writes during backfill.
  • No verification or rollback.
  • Dual writes without handling partial failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why CDC over dual writes? -> A single source of truth for ordering and retry; no partial-failure window in the app.
  2. Where is the commit point? -> The cutover flip; before it everything is reversible.
  3. How do you verify with live data changing? -> Compare at a CDC position or checksum after lag is zero, plus shadow reads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "copy and switch". The senior lists CDC catch-up, verification, commit point and rollback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that skipped checksums cut over, then found 0.02% of rows missing after a timezone bug in the copy tool.

questions.contextHtml: A shard is at 1.8 TB of 3 TB disk, growing 100 GB/week, with p99 latency still good. The team plans to "reshard when it gets close". Backfill for this shard takes about 2 weeks and planning another 2 weeks. A PM adds: a marketing campaign in 6 weeks may double the write rate.
questions.promptHtml: When must you start and what would you set up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wait for the 80% alert", leaving less time than the work needs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is growth linear or compounding? How much headroom does the copy itself need (extra disk, IOPS)? Is the campaign increase on writes to this shard?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start planning now; archive cold data to buy time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) at 100 GB/week, 1.2 TB remaining is 12 weeks to full (matches); b) campaign doubles weekly growth to 200 GB, about 6 weeks to full; c) resharding itself needs headroom.
  4. How I'd verify each: Weekly growth from disk metrics, per-table growth, test copy throughput.
  5. Root cause (math): Planning 2 weeks plus backfill 2 weeks plus verification and cutover about 1 week is 5 weeks. With the campaign, full disk is about 6 weeks away; 60% (1.8 TB) is already the alert level and the margin is a single week.
  6. Fix: Start immediately: provision new shards, rehearse the runbook in staging at production scale, archive cold rows to buy time, set alerts at 60% disk/CPU/IOPS with action at 70%, and add a per-shard dashboard (size, QPS, p99, replication lag, top keys). Use generous logical shard counts (1,024 or 4,096) in the next layout.
  7. Prevention: Written capacity policy, quarterly forecast review, a game day for resharding.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Early resharding costs money for idle capacity; I accept it. I would not wait for a 90% page, and not treat resharding as a single script.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if growth is 15% month on month? -> 60% to 100% in about 4 months, so plan within 1 month.
  • Can you buy time cheaply? -> Archive, compress, drop unused indexes, bigger disk if the platform allows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shard hit 95% disk in the middle of a copy; the copy needed temp space that did not exist and the migration was aborted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reacts at an alert near full.
  • Hire: computes time to full and the migration lead time.
  • Strong hire: includes campaign effect, rehearsal, headroom for the copy and a policy.

questions.contextHtml:
You are moving from 4 to 8 shards (2 TB, 500 GB per old shard) with hash(user_id) into 1,024 logical shards. The plan: backfill, then flip. Rehearsal in staging found a discrepancy: after cutover, 1,900 rows written during the copy are missing from the new shards.

backfill: 500 GB at 40 MB/s = ~3.5 h per shard
snapshot at 02:00:00; cutover at 05:40:00
new shard row count: 123,410,022   old: 123,411,922   diff: 1,900
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and what is the corrected plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the copy again just before cutover", which still leaves a gap and a long pause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is binlog/WAL retention long enough for 4 hours? Can updates and deletes happen? What pause at cutover is acceptable (seconds)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable to production yet. In staging, mark the plan as unsafe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) no change capture after the snapshot: writes during the 3.5 h backfill are missing (1,900 rows); b) deletes/updates also missed (check); c) copy tool bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the missing row timestamps to the window after 02:00; diff by primary key range; check updates via checksum per chunk.
  5. Root cause: Backfill alone copies a point-in-time view; changes after the snapshot were never replicated.
  6. Fix: Take the snapshot and record the log position; run CDC from that position (Debezium, VReplication, logical replication) concurrently so new shards converge; verify via counts and chunk checksums at zero lag; shadow-read a sample; cut over per logical shard with a 3 s write pause behind a router flag (shard_map.state MIGRATING to ACTIVE); keep reverse replication for a week.
  7. Prevention: Rehearsal at production scale as a required gate, automated diff job, runbook with explicit abort and rollback.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: CDC needs binlog retention and extra load on the source; backfill throttles. I would not do app-level dual writes unless there is an outbox, because a failed second write silently diverges.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Post-cutover bug found a day later? -> Reverse replication allows flipping back without losing new writes.
  • The source binlog rotated during backfill? -> Increase retention first; otherwise the snapshot position is lost and the copy must restart.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration passed the row count check but not the checksum check; a collation difference had changed how some keys compared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: re-copy before cutover.
  • Hire: adds CDC from the snapshot position and verification.
  • Strong hire: per-logical-shard cutover, reverse replication, binlog retention and rehearsal gate.

questions.contextHtml: You create a new Elasticsearch index for logs: 3 TB now, expected 12 TB in two years, 6 data nodes (2 TB disk each) growing to maybe 24. A colleague proposes 3 primary shards ("one per two nodes, keep it simple"); another proposes 5,000 shards "so we never reshard". Target shard size guidance: tens of GB (verify current vendor guidance, commonly 10 to 50 GB).
questions.promptHtml: What shard count do you choose and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either extreme with no sizing math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it time-based (could use rollover indices)? Query pattern (fan-out per query)? Retention? Replica count?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) 3 shards: 12 TB / 3 = 4 TB each, far too large, slow recovery and cannot use 24 nodes; b) 5,000 shards: 12 TB / 5,000 = 2.4 GB each, high per-shard memory/file handle overhead and every query fans out to thousands of shards; c) pick for the target: 12 TB / 40 GB = 300 shards or fewer with rollover.
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark query latency at 100, 300 and 1,000 shards on a sample, watch heap and cluster state size.
  5. Root cause of the trade-off: The primary count is fixed at creation (effectively a one-way door, needs reindex/split), too few caps parallelism and recovery time, too many costs memory.
  6. Fix: Use time-based indices with rollover (for example 1 index per day with 6 primary shards of about 30 GB) via ILM, so the count is chosen per index and can change for future indices; keep total shards in the low thousands at most; number of primaries a multiple of node count for even spread.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of shard sizes, ILM policies, alert on shard count per node.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Rollover adds index management but gives adjustable layout; I would not use 3 shards nor 5,000.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data not time-based (search index of products)? -> Pick primaries for the 2-year size, plan the split API or reindex as the escape hatch.
  • Each query hits all shards, is that a problem? -> Fan-out cost grows with shards; limit by index patterns/time ranges.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cluster with 40,000 tiny shards spent most of its heap on cluster state and master elections became slow.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arbitrary number.
  • Hire: sizes shards to tens of GB with math.
  • Strong hire: rollover indices, notes the fixed-at-creation door and fan-out cost.

questions.contextHtml:
A 12-node cluster with automatic rebalancing. During a busy Saturday, a 40 s network blip made node 7 look dead. The cluster began re-replicating its 600 GB to other nodes. Node 7 came back after 2 minutes. Timeline and metrics:

19:02 node7 unreachable (blip, 40s)
19:02 cluster marks node7 down, starts re-replicating its partitions
19:03 node7 back; cluster continues streaming (no cancel)
19:05 p99 latency 25ms -> 1,400ms on 8 nodes; disk util 98%, network 85%
19:20 two more nodes slow, marked down -> more streaming (cascade)
19:45 manual: set rebalance throttle to 20MB/s and delay timeout to 10 min; recovery at 20:30
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, contributing factors and corrective actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The network blip caused it", ignoring the configuration that turned a 40 s blip into a 90 minute outage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was the failure detection timeout and was a delay for re-replication configured? Was the stream throttled? Could the cluster cancel work when the node returned?
  2. Immediate mitigation: What the team did: throttle streaming, increase the delay before treating a node as lost. Better: pause rebalancing completely and let the returned node rejoin with its data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) aggressive failure detection plus immediate re-replication; b) no throttling so streaming starved foreground traffic; c) high disk utilization before the event (no headroom); d) cascade when slow nodes were mis-detected as dead.
  4. How I'd verify each: Timeline from logs, config diff (delayed timeout, throttle), disk and network graphs per node.
  5. Root cause: The cluster treated a transient failure as permanent and moved 600 GB while serving peak traffic, with no throttle. Copy load made healthy nodes look unhealthy, which triggered more copying.
  6. Fix: Delay re-replication (for example 5 to 10 minutes, so short blips and restarts do not trigger copies), throttle recovery to a fraction of the link (for example 20 to 30%), limit concurrent recoveries per node, cancel the move when the original node returns, keep disk below 60 to 70% so there is headroom.
  7. Prevention: Game day with a node-kill and a partition, alert on recovery throughput, dashboards for pending relocations, require human approval for large rebalances at peak.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A longer delay lengthens the window with fewer replicas (more risk if another node fails); I accept it with RF=3. I would not disable automatic recovery entirely, and I would not blame the network team.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if node 7 really died? -> After the delay, recovery starts, throttled, with an alert to a human.
  • Why did healthy nodes fail health checks? -> Disk and CPU saturated by streaming; health checks should be separate from data-plane saturation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Raising a delayed-allocation timeout from 1 to 10 minutes eliminated most storms with no measurable durability change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network.
  • Hire: identifies unthrottled auto re-replication and the cascade.
  • Strong hire: sets delay, throttle, concurrency limits and drills; discusses the durability trade-off.
